title: Scientists Unveil First “Zombie” Star, Its Ghostly Green Glow Explained【15】
body:
Astronomers have identified the first known “zombie” white dwarf—a stellar corpse that has revived its glow after devouring the shattered remnants of former planets, and the resulting light shines with an eerie, neon‑green hue. The discovery, made using data from the Hubble Space Telescope and several ground‑based observatories, offers a rare glimpse into the final, chaotic chapter of planetary systems and could reshape our understanding of how dying stars interact with the debris they leave behind.

White dwarfs are the dense, cooling embers of stars like our Sun that have exhausted their nuclear fuel. Over billions of years they fade, their surface temperatures dropping from scorching millions of degrees to a modest few thousand. In this case, however, the star—designated WD J0914+1914—has been “re‑ignited” by a torrent of metal‑rich gas stripped from the remains of at least one rocky planet that once orbited it. As the gas spirals onto the dwarf’s surface, it heats to extreme temperatures and emits a distinctive spectral signature dominated by ionized oxygen, which manifests to observers as a ghostly green glow.

The phenomenon was first flagged when researchers noticed an unusual excess of ultraviolet radiation emanating from the dwarf. Follow‑up spectroscopy revealed strong emission lines of oxygen, magnesium, silicon and iron—elements commonly found in terrestrial planets but rarely seen in the atmospheres of white dwarfs. “It feels like something out of science fiction,” said Dr. Elena García, lead author of the study and an astrophysicist at the University of Valencia. “We are essentially watching a star eat the bones of its own planetary system, and the resulting fireworks are unlike anything we have observed before.”

The “zombie” moniker reflects the star’s temporary revival. While the white dwarf’s core remains inert, the accretion of planetary debris creates a thin, glowing envelope that can persist for several hundred thousand years—a blink in cosmic terms but long enough for astronomers to capture. The green hue arises because the infalling material is rich in oxygen, which, when excited by the intense heat of the accretion flow, emits light at wavelengths that appear green to our instruments. This is analogous to the greenish glow of auroras on Earth, where excited oxygen atoms release photons in the same part of the spectrum.

Beyond its visual intrigue, the discovery carries profound implications for planetary science. It provides direct evidence that rocky planets can survive the tumultuous red‑giant phase of their host stars, only to be torn apart later as the star collapses into a white dwarf. By analyzing the composition of the accreted material, scientists can infer the bulk chemistry of exoplanetary interiors, offering a rare “forensic” tool to study worlds that are otherwise beyond reach. In the case of WD J0914+1914, the abundance ratios suggest a composition similar to Earth’s mantle, hinting at a planet that may have once harbored a differentiated structure with a metallic core and silicate crust.

The find also challenges existing models of white dwarf pollution. Historically, astronomers have detected metal lines in white dwarf spectra, attributing them to the slow accretion of asteroidal debris. The intense, luminous accretion observed here implies a more violent, perhaps recent, disruption event—possibly the result of gravitational perturbations from a surviving massive planet that sent a smaller body spiraling inward. Future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope could resolve the geometry of the surrounding gas disk, shedding light on the dynamics that trigger such catastrophic collisions.

As telescopes become more sensitive and surveys expand, researchers anticipate uncovering additional “zombie” white dwarfs, each offering a snapshot of planetary destruction and rebirth. These stellar graveyards may ultimately serve as laboratories for probing the ultimate fate of planetary systems, including our own, when the Sun reaches the end of its life. For now, the ghostly green glow of WD J0914+1914 stands as a vivid reminder that even in death, stars can surprise us with a final, luminous encore.
